title: Equations Using Identities
subject: mathematics

theory.introduction: Many difficult trigonometric equations cannot be solved directly. The key is to transform them into a familiar form using identities. The most important skill is not merely memorizing identities, but recognizing which identity will simplify the equation. A good transformation usually reduces the number of different trigonometric functions, reduces the complexity of the expression, creates a factorable or quadratic form, or converts the equation into one of the basic equations already learned.

content.text: Do not apply identities randomly. First inspect the equation and identify what is preventing it from being solved directly.

If both sin(x) and cos(x) appear, a Pythagorean identity may allow one function to be eliminated. If sec(x), csc(x), or cot(x) appears, reciprocal identities can convert the equation into sine, cosine, or tangent. If sin²(x) and cos²(x) appear together, the Pythagorean identity is often useful.

If expressions contain 2x, 3x, or another multiple angle, double-angle or multiple-angle identities may simplify them. If sums such as sin(A + B) or cos(A − B) appear, sum-and-difference identities may be required.
The goal is always to transform the equation into a form that can be solved using algebra, factoring, quadratic methods, or the basic trigonometric equations from earlier lessons.

This lesson is the central identity reference for the equation module. Learn how to recognize and select an identity, but later equation lessons should use the required identity as a tool rather than reteaching the identity library.
Pythagorean identities are among the most important identities in trigonometric equation solving. They allow squared trigonometric functions to be converted into each other.
The fundamental identity is sin²(x) + cos²(x) = 1.
Dividing this identity by cos²(x) produces 1 + tan²(x) = sec²(x), while dividing by sin²(x) produces 1 + cot²(x) = csc²(x).
These identities are particularly useful when an equation contains squared trigonometric functions or when you need to eliminate one type of function.
Reciprocal identities connect each basic trigonometric function with its reciprocal.
They are useful when an equation mixes functions such as sec(x) and cos(x), or csc(x) and sin(x).
A common strategy is to rewrite every function using sine and cosine when this produces a simpler equation.
Tangent and cotangent can be rewritten using sine and cosine.
This is useful when an equation contains a mixture of tan(x), sin(x), and cos(x), because rewriting tangent may allow the entire equation to be expressed using only sine and cosine.
Even and odd identities describe how trigonometric functions behave when their input is replaced by its negative.
They can simplify equations containing negative angles and are especially useful when expressions such as sin(−x), cos(−x), or tan(−x) appear.
Cofunction identities relate trigonometric functions of complementary angles.
For example, sin(π/2 − x) = cos(x). These identities can transform an equation into one involving a single trigonometric function.
Sum-and-difference identities expand expressions involving angles such as A + B and A − B.
They are particularly useful when an equation contains expressions such as sin(x + π/3), cos(x − π/4), or products involving known special angles.
They can also convert an unfamiliar angle expression into combinations of sin(x) and cos(x).
Double-angle identities connect expressions involving 2x with expressions involving x.
For cosine there are three especially useful forms: cos(2x) = cos²(x) − sin²(x), cos(2x) = 2cos²(x) − 1, and cos(2x) = 1 − 2sin²(x).
The choice of form matters. Choose the version that matches the functions already present in the equation.
Double-angle identities are particularly important for converting between multiple-angle equations and quadratic equations.
Power-reduction identities express squared sine and cosine in terms of cos(2x).
These are especially useful when an equation contains sin²(x) or cos²(x) and also contains a multiple-angle expression.
They can transform a quadratic-looking equation into a linear equation in cos(2x), or transform a multiple-angle expression into squared functions.
Triple-angle identities express sin(3x) and cos(3x) using powers of sin(x) or cos(x).
They can be useful when solving equations containing 3x or when converting a multiple-angle equation into an algebraic equation.
Because triple-angle equations can generate several solutions, interval checking is especially important.
Half-angle identities express trigonometric functions of x/2 in terms of functions of x.
They are useful when an equation contains angles such as x/2 or when solving equations involving squared trigonometric functions and a change of angle is helpful.
The ± sign in square-root forms must be handled carefully because the sign depends on the quadrant of the angle.
Product-to-sum identities convert products of sine and cosine functions into sums or differences.
They are useful when an equation contains products such as sin(A)cos(B), cos(A)cos(B), or sin(A)sin(B) and an additive form is easier to solve.
These identities are more specialized than the core Pythagorean and double-angle identities, but they can be essential for certain advanced equation-solving problems.
Sum-to-product identities convert sums or differences of trigonometric functions into products.
They are particularly useful when the resulting product can be set equal to zero and solved using the Zero Product Property.
An identity often does not solve an equation by itself. Its purpose may be to transform the equation into a factorable form.
For example, sin²(x) − sin(x) = 0 can be factored directly, while an equation involving both sin²(x) and cos²(x) may first require the Pythagorean identity before factoring.
This creates an important problem-solving pattern: identity → algebraic simplification → factoring → basic trigonometric equations.
Identities can transform equations into quadratic form.
For example, replacing sin²(x) with 1 − cos²(x) can turn an equation into a quadratic in cos(x).
This directly connects identity manipulation with the quadratic trigonometric equations studied in the previous lesson.

When an equation needs an identity, identify the target form first, apply the smallest useful identity transformation, solve the resulting trigonometric equation, and check the original equation when necessary. Multiple-angle equation mechanics are applied in trig-equations-08; general-solution notation is consolidated in trig-equations-11.
Some identities involve division by sin(x) or cos(x). The resulting identity is therefore interpreted on the domain where those divisions are defined.
For example, tan(x) = sin(x)/cos(x) requires cos(x) ≠ 0, while sec(x) = 1/cos(x) also requires cos(x) ≠ 0.
Never forget the original domain of the equation when rewriting expressions using reciprocals or quotient identities.
sin²(x) and cos²(x) together → try the Pythagorean identity.
tan²(x) and sec²(x) together → try 1 + tan²(x) = sec²(x).
cot²(x) and csc²(x) together → try 1 + cot²(x) = csc²(x).
sec(x), csc(x), or cot(x) mixed with sine and cosine → try reciprocal identities.
tan(x) mixed with sine and cosine → try quotient identities.
Expressions involving 2x → try double-angle identities.
Squared sine or cosine → consider power-reduction or Pythagorean identities depending on the target form.
Expressions involving A + B or A − B → try sum-and-difference identities.
Products of trigonometric functions → consider product-to-sum identities.
Sums or differences of trigonometric functions → consider sum-to-product identities.
Expressions involving 3x → consider triple-angle identities.

formulas.explanation: One of the most important identities in trigonometric equation solving. Use it to convert between sin²(x) and cos²(x), eliminate one function, or create quadratic form.

formulas.name: [IMPORTANT FOR PROBLEM SOLVING] Identity Principle
formulas.expression: If A(x) = B(x) is an identity, either side can replace the other wherever the identity is valid.
formulas.explanation: The fundamental principle behind identity-based equation solving. Choose the form that makes the equation easier to solve.

examples.question: Solve 1 − 2sin²(x) = 0 for 0 ≤ x < 2π.
examples.solution: Recognize the double-angle identity cos(2x) = 1 − 2sin²(x). Therefore cos(2x) = 0. Let y = 2x. Then cos(y) = 0, so y = π/2 + nπ. Thus 2x = π/2 + nπ, giving x = π/4 + nπ/2. On 0 ≤ x < 2π, the solutions are x = π/4, 3π/4, 5π/4, 7π/4.

examples.question: Solve sin²(x) + cos(x) = 0 for 0 ≤ x < 2π.
examples.solution: Use sin²(x) = 1 − cos²(x). Then 1 − cos²(x) + cos(x) = 0. Rearrange: cos²(x) − cos(x) − 1 = 0. Let u = cos(x). The quadratic formula gives u = (1 ± √5)/2. The value (1 + √5)/2 is greater than 1 and is impossible for cosine. Therefore cos(x) = (1 − √5)/2. Solve this cosine equation on the required interval.

examples.question: Solve sin²(x) − sin(x) = 0 for 0 ≤ x < 2π.
examples.solution: Factor directly: sin(x)(sin(x) − 1) = 0. Therefore sin(x) = 0 or sin(x) = 1. This gives x = 0, π and x = π/2. Final answer: x = 0, π/2, π.

examples.question: Solve sec(x) = 2 for 0 ≤ x < 2π.
examples.solution: Use the reciprocal identity sec(x) = 1/cos(x). Then 1/cos(x) = 2, so cos(x) = 1/2. Therefore x = π/3 or 5π/3.

examples.question: Solve tan(x) = sin(x)/cos(x) for all x where both sides are defined.
examples.solution: The quotient identity tan(x) = sin(x)/cos(x) is an identity, meaning the two expressions are equal everywhere on their common domain. The common domain requires cos(x) ≠ 0.

examples.question: Solve sin(2x) = sin(x) for 0 ≤ x < 2π.
examples.solution: Use sin(2x) = 2sin(x)cos(x). Then 2sin(x)cos(x) = sin(x). Move everything to one side: 2sin(x)cos(x) − sin(x) = 0. Factor: sin(x)(2cos(x) − 1) = 0. Therefore sin(x) = 0 or cos(x) = 1/2. On 0 ≤ x < 2π, this gives x = 0, π, π/3, 5π/3.

examples.question: Solve cos(2x) = cos(x) for 0 ≤ x < 2π.
examples.solution: Use cos(2x) = 2cos²(x) − 1. Then 2cos²(x) − 1 = cos(x). Rearrange: 2cos²(x) − cos(x) − 1 = 0. Factor: (2cos(x) + 1)(cos(x) − 1) = 0. Therefore cos(x) = −1/2 or cos(x) = 1. On 0 ≤ x < 2π, the solutions are x = 2π/3, 4π/3, 0.

examples.question: Solve sin(x + π/3) = √3/2 for 0 ≤ x < 2π.
examples.solution: Let y = x + π/3. Then sin(y) = √3/2. Therefore y = π/3 + 2nπ or y = 2π/3 + 2nπ. Subtract π/3 from each family: x = 2nπ or x = π/3 + 2nπ. On 0 ≤ x < 2π, x = 0 and π/3.

examples.question: Solve sin(x) + sin(3x) = 0 for 0 ≤ x < 2π.
examples.solution: Use sin(A) + sin(B) = 2sin((A+B)/2)cos((A−B)/2). This gives 2sin(2x)cos(−x) = 0. Since cos(−x) = cos(x), the equation becomes 2sin(2x)cos(x) = 0. Therefore sin(2x) = 0 or cos(x) = 0. Solving both gives the complete set of solutions in the required interval.

examples.question: Solve sec²(x) − tan²(x) = 1 for all x in the common domain.
examples.solution: Use the Pythagorean identity sec²(x) − tan²(x) = 1. The equation is therefore an identity and is true for every x for which sec(x) and tan(x) are defined. Since both require cos(x) ≠ 0, the solution set is all x such that x ≠ π/2 + nπ, n ∈ ℤ.

examples.question: Solve 1 + tan²(x) = 4 for 0 ≤ x < 2π.
examples.solution: Recognize the Pythagorean identity 1 + tan²(x) = sec²(x), giving sec²(x) = 4. Thus sec(x) = ±2. Using sec(x) = 1/cos(x), cos(x) = ±1/2. Therefore x = π/3, 2π/3, 4π/3, 5π/3.

examples.question: Rewrite 3 − 2cos²(x) using a double-angle identity.
examples.solution: Use 2cos²(x) − 1 = cos(2x). Therefore 3 − 2cos²(x) = 3 − [cos(2x) + 1] = 2 − cos(2x). The important skill is choosing the double-angle form that matches cos²(x).

examples.question: Explain why an identity transformation must preserve the original domain.
examples.solution: Consider tan(x) = sin(x)/cos(x). This equality is valid only where cos(x) ≠ 0 because tan(x) is undefined when cos(x) = 0. Therefore replacing tan(x) with sin(x)/cos(x) does not make those excluded values valid. Domain restrictions from the original equation must always be preserved.

key_ideas: The purpose of an identity is to transform an equation into a form that is easier to solve.
Do not use identities randomly; choose one based on the structure of the equation.
The Pythagorean identities are among the most important identities for problem solving.
Reciprocal identities are useful for converting sec, csc, and cot into basic trigonometric functions.
Quotient identities are useful for converting tan and cot into sine and cosine.
Double-angle identities are essential when equations contain 2x or products such as sin(x)cos(x).
Power-reduction identities are useful when squared sine or cosine expressions need to be converted into double-angle expressions.
Sum-to-product identities can turn an equation into a factorable product.
Product-to-sum identities can turn products into sums or differences.
Pythagorean identities can convert equations into quadratic form.
Identity manipulation and factoring often work together.
Identity manipulation and quadratic methods often work together.
After transforming an equation, return to the basic trigonometric equations whenever possible.
Every resulting factor or trigonometric equation must be solved.
General solutions and restricted-interval solutions must be handled separately.
Domain restrictions must be preserved during identity transformations.
The best identity is the one that moves the equation closer to a familiar solvable form.
Some identities are far more frequently used in problem solving than others; these are explicitly marked as important.
misconceptions: Trying random identities without first identifying the desired target form.
Assuming that applying more identities always makes an equation easier.
Memorizing identities without understanding what type of expression each identity transforms.
Forgetting the rearranged forms of the Pythagorean identity.
Using the wrong double-angle form for the functions present in the equation.
Forgetting that sin²(x) and cos²(x) are squared functions, not sin(x²) and cos(x²).
Applying a reciprocal identity without considering where the reciprocal function is undefined.
Dividing by sin(x) or cos(x) and losing possible solutions.
Forgetting that sum-to-product identities are useful because they create factors.
Stopping after applying an identity instead of solving the resulting equation.
Finding only one angle from a transformed trigonometric equation.
Forgetting to account for the full interval after a multiple-angle substitution.
Ignoring the ± sign in half-angle square-root identities.
Using half-angle identities without determining the correct sign from the quadrant.
Forgetting that an identity may only be valid on a restricted common domain.
Assuming that an identity transformation automatically preserves values where the transformed expression is undefined.
Checking only the transformed equation instead of the original equation when division or another potentially non-reversible operation was used.
